# Search and rescue: detection, coverage and the best use of effort

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2)
library(rmoriebricklayer)
```

Search theory began with Koopman's work for the U.S. Navy (1946) and is how search and rescue
services plan a search: how likely a sensor is to see the object at a given distance, how
much ground a search covers, how likely the object is to be in each area, and where a limited
effort does the most good. Frost's *The Theory of Search: A Simplified Explanation* (1996)
explains it for search planners in four chapters of figures. This vignette walks those
chapters and draws every one of the book's 36 figures with `srchfig()`, which builds each from
the package's functions with the book's parameters. `srchfig()` with no argument lists them
and says how each is drawn: from the model, as a schematic, or as an approximation where the
book's plate cannot be recovered exactly.

```{r search-and-rescue-list}
table(srchfig()$how)
```

The functions behind the figures work on any inputs: `ltrlrng()` (lateral range curves),
`swpwdth()` (sweep width), `srchpod()` and `pswppod()` (probability of detection),
`srchscs()` (probability of success and the update after a search), `datumpmap()` (where
the object may be), `opteffort()`, `optcrcsrch()` and `optsqr()` (the best use of effort). The book's figures
come first; [Your own search](#your-own-search) then runs each function on numbers of your own.

## Datums and probability maps

**Figure 3-1.** A point datum is a circular normal distribution of possible positions. The
probability that the object is within `R` standard deviations of the datum is
`POC = 1 - exp(-R^2 / 2)`.

```{r search-and-rescue-f31}
srchfig("3-1")
```

**Figures 3-2, 3-3 and 3-5.** The square circumscribed about a circle of radius `R` holds
`(2 Phi(R) - 1)^2` of the distribution: 47% for one standard deviation, 58% for the total
probable error of position `E = sqrt(2 ln 2) = 1.1774` standard deviations (the radius
holding 50%), and 65% for the simplified method's first search radius of 1.1 `E`.

```{r search-and-rescue-f32}
srchfig("3-2")
srchfig("3-3")
srchfig("3-5")
```

**Figure 3-4.** A probability map lays a grid over the distribution. With cells `2E` wide the
centre holds 57.91%, a side cell 9.08% and a corner 1.42%.

```{r search-and-rescue-f34}
srchfig("3-4")
```

**Figures 3-6 and 3-7.** The simplified method extended a point datum to a line by drawing
circles at the two end points and boxing them in. The density this implies is drawn as a
circular normal spread along the segment (`datum = "line"`), an approximation of the book's
plate.

```{r search-and-rescue-f36}
srchfig("3-6")
srchfig("3-7")
```

**Figures 3-8 to 3-10.** A simpler line datum is normal across the line and uniform along it,
with nothing beyond its ends (`datum = "corridor"`). A strip one standard deviation either
side holds 68%, a strip of `2E` holds 76.1%, and dividing strips into cells along the line
gives the completed map of figure 3-10.

```{r search-and-rescue-f38}
srchfig("3-8")
srchfig("3-9")
srchfig("3-10")
```

**Figures 3-11 and 3-12.** An area datum spreads the probability evenly: each of 20 equal
cells holds 5%.

```{r search-and-rescue-f311}
srchfig("3-11")
srchfig("3-12")
```

**Figures 3-13 and 3-14.** A generalized datum takes the planner's own cell probabilities
(`datum = "general"`, `wts =`). The book's surface is illustrative; here it is drawn from the
cells of figure 3-14.

```{r search-and-rescue-f313}
srchfig("3-13")
srchfig("3-14")
```

## Lateral range curves and sweep width

**Figure 4-1.** A lateral range curve `p(x)` is the probability of detecting an object that
passes at distance `x` from the track. The sweep width is its area,
`W = integral of p(x) dx`; the dashed rectangles have the same area.

```{r search-and-rescue-f41, fig.height = 5}
srchfig("4-1")
```

**Figures 4-2 and 4-3.** A definite range sensor sees everything within `W / 2` of its track
and nothing beyond: it sweeps a strip exactly `W` wide.

```{r search-and-rescue-f42}
srchfig("4-2")
srchfig("4-3")
```

**Figures 4-4 and 4-5.** The M-Beta curve has height `M` over a width of `W / M`; with
`M = 0.5` and `M = 0.25` the sweep width is unchanged.

```{r search-and-rescue-f44}
srchfig("4-4")
srchfig("4-5")
```

**Figures 4-6 and 4-7.** Koopman's inverse cube law takes the chance of a glimpse to be
proportional to the solid angle of the wake, `k h / r^3`, which gives
`p(x) = 1 - exp(-W^2 / (4 pi x^2))`. Its sweep width is `W`: the objects missed inside the
sweep width (A) balance those seen outside it (B).

```{r search-and-rescue-f46}
srchfig("4-6")
srchfig("4-7")
swpwdth(ltrlrng(seq(-500, 500, by = 0.01), W = 1))
```

## Effort, coverage and probability of detection

**Figure 5-1.** Search effort is sweep width times track length, `Z = W L`, and coverage is
effort over area, `C = Z / A`. A search whose path is random gives `POD = 1 - exp(-C)`.

```{r search-and-rescue-f51}
srchfig("5-1")
```

**Figures 5-2 to 5-5.** A parallel sweep at track spacing `S` has coverage `C = W / S`. With
a definite range sensor the POD is `min(C, 1)`: half the gap is seen at `S = 2W`, all of it at
`S = W`.

```{r search-and-rescue-f52}
srchfig("5-2")
srchfig("5-3")
srchfig("5-4")
srchfig("5-5")
```

**Figures 5-6 and 5-7.** M-Beta curves overlap once the tracks are closer than their width:
`POD = C` below `C = M` and `1 - (1 - M)^(C / M)` above it, 0.75 and 0.6836 at coverage 1
for `M = 0.5` and `M = 0.25`, nearer the random search curve as `M` falls.

```{r search-and-rescue-f56}
srchfig("5-6")
srchfig("5-7")
srchpod(c(0.5, 1, 2), "mbeta", m = 0.25)
```

**Figure 5-8.** The inverse cube parallel sweep gives `POD = erf(sqrt(pi) C / 2)`, 0.7899 at
coverage 1, between the definite range and random search curves. `pswppod()` computes the
same sweep directly, for any curve.

```{r search-and-rescue-f58}
srchfig("5-8")
pswppod(W = 1, S = 1)
```

**Figure 5-9.** Poorer conditions shrink the sweep width, and a cross-track navigation error
of standard deviation `sigma` flattens the curve: the expected curve is the convolution
`phi(x) = integral of p(x - t) Z(t, sigma) dt`, whose area is still `W`
(`ltrlrng(..., navsd = )`). The plate is blank in the published file; it is drawn from the
text.

```{r search-and-rescue-f59}
srchfig("5-9")
```

## Optimal search

**Figures 6-1 and 6-2.** With half the probability in a 3 by 3 square inside a 5 by 5 one
and effort for half the area, the trial squares of the whole area, half of it and a third of
it hold 100%, 60.94% and 46.30%; at coverage 1 the middle trial succeeds most often.

```{r search-and-rescue-f61}
srchfig("6-1")
srchfig("6-2")
```

**Figures 6-3 and 6-4.** For a point datum, `optsqr()` finds the square that an effort,
spread evenly, should cover: the search factor is its half side in units of `E`. An effort of
`4 E^2` gives a factor of 1.02, coverage 0.96 and POS 0.4578, as the book's program found.

```{r search-and-rescue-f63}
optsqr(4)
srchfig("6-3")
srchfig("6-4")
```

**Figure 6-5.** By the additive principle, a series of searches each optimal for what the
earlier ones left does as well as one optimal search with all the effort: the cumulative
probability of success depends on the cumulative effort.

```{r search-and-rescue-f65}
srchfig("6-5")
```

**Figure 6-6.** Searching in a series with random efforts between 0.1 and 50 `E^2`, the
optimal factors cluster around the curve, except where a much smaller effort follows a large
one and the best use of it is the remaining central peak.

```{r search-and-rescue-f66}
srchfig("6-6")
```

## Your own search

The figures use the book's numbers; every function takes yours, and each result has a `plot()`
method. Say a sensor's sweep width is 0.8 nautical miles and its detection falls off as the
inverse cube of the lateral range. Its lateral range curve, and the picture of what the sweep
width means (the objects missed inside it equal those seen outside it, Figure 4-7):

```{r search-and-rescue-own-lateral}
lr <- ltrlrng(seq(-3, 3, by = 0.05), W = 0.8)
plot(lr)
plot(lr, equiv = TRUE)
```

A sweep width can also come from a field trial: the share of objects detected at each lateral
range, measured on both sides of the track. `swpwdth()` integrates the curve.

```{r search-and-rescue-own-sweep}
d <- c(-3, -2, -1.5, -1, -0.5, -0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3)
p <- c(0.01, 0.08, 0.2, 0.45, 0.75, 0.9, 0.95, 0.9, 0.75, 0.45, 0.2, 0.08, 0.01)
swpwdth(d, p)
```

The probability of detection for the coverage a plan gives (coverage is sweep width times track
length over the area), and for parallel sweeps at a track spacing of 1 with a navigation error
of 0.1:

```{r search-and-rescue-own-pod}
pd <- srchpod(seq(0, 3, by = 0.1), model = "invcube")
plot(pd)
pswppod(W = 0.8, S = 1, navsd = 0.1)
```

After a search of three areas that found nothing, the chance the object is in each area is
updated by what each search could have detected:

```{r search-and-rescue-own-update}
srchscs(poc = c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2), pod = c(0.8, 0.5, 0))
```

## On a grid of your own

The same functions take any grid and datum. `opteffort()` spreads a total track length over
the cells to make the probability of success as large as possible (Stone 1975), and
`srchscs()` updates the containment after a search that finds nothing.

```{r search-and-rescue-grid}
m <- datumpmap(seq(-6, 6, by = 0.5), seq(-6, 6, by = 0.5), sigma = 2)
a <- opteffort(m, W = 1, effort = 30)
a$pos
optcrcsrch(sigma = 2, W = 1, effort = 30)$pos
plot(a)
srchscs(c(0.5, 0.3, 0.2), c(0.8, 0.5, 0))
```

## References

Frost, J. R. (1996). The Theory of Search: A Simplified Explanation. Soza and Company and
U.S. Coast Guard Office of Search and Rescue. Chapters 3-6 and their figures.

Koopman, B. O. (1946). Search and Screening. OEG Report 56, Office of the Chief of Naval
Operations.

Koopman, B. O. (1956-1957). The theory of search, parts I-III. Operations Research 4(3),
324-346; 4(5), 503-531; 5(5), 613-626.

Stone, L. D. (1975). Theory of Optimal Search. Academic Press.
